summary: A document from the Network Graphics Group describing part of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol for sending graphics from a serving host to a display package at a using host. The protocol was a stream of 8-bit bytes called the graphics output byte stream. It reflects decisions from a late-1971 meeting and obsoletes RFC 292.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 493 proposes a byte-stream format for sending drawing commands from one host to a graphics display on another. It covers graphics output, groups features into levels and leaves several display details to implementations.

subtitle: An experimental byte-stream protocol for drawing graphics on a remote console.

tldr.problem: An application on one host needed a defined way to send graphics output to a console at another host.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal encodes drawing commands and their arguments in an 8-bit byte stream, with commands grouped into progressively richer levels.
tldr.outcome: The document is a basis for discussion and experimentation, covers output only, and obsoletes RFC 292.

today: RFC 493 obsoletes RFC 292, and its status is listed as Unknown. The RFC describes the protocol as a proposal for discussion and experimentation.

sections.title: What the Graphics Protocol Covers
sections.content:
RFC 493 describes part of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol. It covers graphics output sent from an application on a Serving Host to a display package at a Using Host. The output is a stream of 8-bit bytes.

The document does not define graphics input from the Using Host or how the hosts establish their connection. It is intended as a basis for discussion and experimentation, and does not provide a way for the display host to report logical errors in the output stream.
sections.plainLanguage: This proposal sends drawing instructions one way, from the host creating graphics to the host displaying them. It does not cover input or connection setup.

sections.title: Commands, Arguments and Coordinates
sections.content:
A command consists of a command byte followed by zero or more arguments. A value is an 8-bit integer; a string is a count followed by that many 8-bit bytes. The protocol uses a two-dimensional logical coordinate system, with the origin at the center of the screen, and leaves each display interpreter to map logical coordinates to its physical device.

The proposal uses two bytes per coordinate initially and represents text with Network ASCII. It describes absolute positions and relative movements, which specify a position in relation to the current beam position.
sections.plainLanguage: Each instruction starts with a command and may include values, text or coordinates. The receiving display translates the shared logical coordinates to its own screen.

sections.title: The Basic Drawing Commands
sections.content:
Level 0 is designed to be simple enough for less powerful hosts or programmable terminals. It includes commands to erase and reset the beam, move it, draw a line, display a dot, display text, end a picture and pass device-specific bytes through. Move, draw and dot commands have absolute and relative forms.

ERASE starts a new picture and must be paired with ENDPIC. TEXTR displays text and restores the beam position; the RFC discourages the plain TEXT command in favor of TEXTR.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic level can clear the screen, move a drawing point, draw lines and dots, and display text. A picture starts with ERASE and ends with ENDPIC.

sections.title: Higher Levels and Unspecified Behavior
sections.content:
Each higher level includes the lower levels. Level 1 adds line modes, intensity, formatted text and subpictures. Level 2 adds a stack for saved beam positions and allows multiple levels of simple subpicture calls. Level 3 adds full subpictures that can be translated, rotated or scaled. Level 4 adds viewports that display subpictures within portions of the logical screen.

The proposal leaves some behavior unspecified, including how graphics beyond screen boundaries are handled. It warns that command codes could be reassigned while the numbering proposal remained unsettled.
sections.plainLanguage: Higher levels add richer drawing features while retaining the simpler levels. The proposal leaves some display behavior open and warns implementers that command numbers might change.
